meta.title: The Weight of the Web
meta.description: Why modern pages got heavy, what that costs users and the planet, and how a performance budget fixes it.
meta.audience: Engineers, designers, and product owners shipping web products
meta.objective: Adopt a measurable performance budget as a release gate.

assets.alt: A page of a book photographed at close range, evoking the idea of a lighter, more careful web.

slides.title: The page you ship has a weight 1

blocks.content: WEB PERFORMANCE · A DATA STORY
The page you ship has a weight.
Every byte you ship travels over a network, costs energy to serve and render, and competes with your user's attention. This talk is about one number that controls all of it: the median page weight.
A practical guide to measuring, budgeting, and shipping lighter pages.

content.title: Median desktop page weight
content.summary: Median desktop page weight grew from about 1.6 megabytes in 2016 to 2.4 megabytes in 2024.

blocks.alt: Bar chart showing median desktop page weight rising from 1.6 MB in 2016 to 2.4 MB in 2024.

slides.speakerNotes: Open with the physical reality behind every page load: bytes, networks, energy, and attention. The median page is not a small file — it is a 2.4 MB download that has to happen before a single sentence is readable.

slides.title: The median page weighs 2.4 MB 2

blocks.content: MEDIAN TOTAL PAGE WEIGHT, DESKTOP
Half of it is images, a quarter is JavaScript.
Images and JavaScript together account for roughly three quarters of the median page's transfer size — and most of its energy cost.
HTTP Archive · Web Almanac, median desktop page weight, 2016–2024 (approximate).

slides.speakerNotes: One number frames the whole talk. Everything that follows is a consequence of this number: network cost, device energy, rendering time, and cognitive load.

slides.title: Pages did not get bigger on purpose 3

blocks.content: FIVE YEARS OF TREND
Pages did not get heavier on purpose.

content.title: Median desktop page weight, by year
content.summary: Median desktop page weight rose nearly every year, from 1.6 MB in 2016 to 2.4 MB in 2024.

blocks.alt: Bar chart of median desktop page weight from 2016 to 2024, climbing steadily to 2.4 megabytes.

blocks.content: No single team made this happen. It is the aggregate of a thousand small, individually reasonable additions.
HTTP Archive, median desktop page weight by year (approximate).

slides.speakerNotes: Nobody adds 'more megabytes' to their backlog. Weight accretes one dependency, one hero image, one tracking script at a time. This is why the fix must be a measurable budget, not a series of individual decisions.

slides.title: Images and JavaScript carry most of the cost 4

blocks.content: ANATOMY OF A MEDIAN PAGE
Images and JavaScript carry most of the cost.

content.title: Share of median page weight
content.summary: Images are about half of median page weight, JavaScript about a quarter, with fonts, CSS, and other resources making up the rest.

blocks.alt: Horizontal bar chart showing images at fifty percent of page weight, JavaScript twenty-five percent, and the rest split among fonts, CSS, and video.

content: Images dominate bytes because most are shipped larger than the rendered size.
JavaScript adds weight twice: download time, then parse and execute time.
Fonts and CSS feel small, but they block first paint.

slides.speakerNotes: Point at the two bars that matter. Images are a delivery problem; JavaScript is a delivery plus execution problem. Fonts and CSS are small but block rendering, which makes them feel expensive out of proportion to their bytes.

slides.title: Budget first, optimize later 5

blocks.content: THE WORKFLOW
Budget first, optimize later.

steps.title: Measure
steps.detail: Track page weight, image bytes, and JS on a real device.

steps.title: Set the number
steps.detail: Pick a budget: e.g. 1.5 MB total, 500 KB JavaScript.

steps.title: Ship lean
steps.detail: Treat budget overruns like test failures, not suggestions.

steps.title: Verify in CI
steps.detail: Fail the build when the budget is exceeded.

steps.title: Repeat monthly
steps.detail: Re-baseline against a real device every month.

blocks.alt: Five-step workflow: measure, set a budget number, ship lean, verify in CI, and repeat monthly.

blocks.content: A budget turns an aspiration ('be faster') into a measurable, enforceable number.

slides.speakerNotes: The performance budget framework, popularized by Tim Kadlec and Google's Web Fundamentals, is the operational heart of the talk. Without a number, performance is a vibe; with a number, it is an engineering constraint.

slides.title: Budget teams ship a different web 6

blocks.content: TWO CULTURES, SAME CODEBASE
Budget teams ship a different web.

content: Adds images in AVIF/WebP, sized to layout.
Challenges new JavaScript with a review.
Treats the budget as a release gate.
Ships smaller bundles and fewer requests.
Adds whatever the design produces.
Ships original-resolution assets.
Optimizes 'when there is time'.
Discovers weight after launch.

blocks.content: Budget-first team
Business-as-usual team
The difference is not skill. It is a decision about when a page is 'done'.

slides.speakerNotes: This comparison is deliberately about culture, not intelligence. Both teams contain the same quality of engineers. The budget team simply has a definition of done that includes a number.

slides.title: Ship a page 40% lighter this sprint 7

blocks.content: YOUR NEXT ACTION
Ship a page 40% lighter this sprint.
Pick one public page. Measure it. Cut 40% of its weight by removing, compressing, or deferring what does not help the user. Then set that number as the budget.
Owner: your team · Do it now · Budget in CI by next sprint
Sources: HTTP Archive, Web Almanac, Web Performance Budgets.

blocks.alt: A page of a book photographed at close range, evoking the idea of a lighter, more careful web.

slides.speakerNotes: End with a specific, testable action. The 'one public page, cut 40%' framing gives a concrete first move that produces a measurable number by the end of a single sprint.
